CHAPTER 6 · LEARNING AREA 6 · NOVEMBER

Normally distributed random variables

Fill quantities of bottles, heights, measurement errors, the number of heads in a thousand coin tosses: the same shape appears again and again, the Gaussian bell curve. You learn to calculate probabilities as areas under a density, to work with the distribution function $\Phi$ and the $\sigma$ rules, and to understand why every binomial distribution with a large $n$ hugs this curve.

10 LESSONS3 UNITS3 WIDGETS1 LAB
WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER
  • describe continuous random variables with a density function: probability is area
  • know the Gaussian bell curve $\varphi_{\mu;\sigma}$ and explain the influence of $\mu$ and $\sigma$, also with derivatives
  • calculate probabilities and limits with the distribution function and by standardising, use the $\sigma$ rules
  • approximate binomial distributions by the normal distribution with the theorem of de Moivre-Laplace and judge the quality

UNIT 14 LESSONS

1Continuous random variables and the bell curve

A height can take any value in an interval, not just whole centimetres. Such a continuous random variable has the probability $0$ for every single value. Only intervals make sense. A histogram with finer and finer classes, whose bar areas are the probabilities, approaches a curve: the density function.

With a density, the area is the probability, not the function value. That is why the whole area under the graph must be $1$. The most important density is Gauss's bell curve. Its maximum is at the expected value $\mu$, its points of inflection lie exactly one standard deviation to the left and right of it. A large $\sigma$ makes the bell wide and flat, because the area stays $1$.

KEY POINT · DENSITY AND NORMAL DISTRIBUTION

A density function $f$ has $f(x) \ge 0$ and $\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x = 1$. For the random variable $X$, $P(a \le X \le b) = \displaystyle\int_a^b f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x$.

$X$ is called normally distributed with the parameters $\mu$ and $\sigma > 0$, in short $X \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)$, if $\varphi_{\mu;\sigma}(x) = \dfrac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\,\mathrm{e}^{-\frac{(x - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}}$ is its density.

Then $E(X) = \mu$, $V(X) = \sigma^2$. The graph is symmetric about $x = \mu$, has its maximum there and points of inflection at $\mu \pm \sigma$.

$\le$ or $<$? For continuous random variables it makes no difference, because $P(X = a) = 0$. For the binomial distribution it makes a big difference.

Standard normal distribution: $\mu = 0$, $\sigma = 1$. Its density is called $\varphi$ for short, its distribution function $\Phi$.

On the CAS: normPdf(x, μ, σ) for the density, normCdf(a, b, μ, σ) for $P(a \le X \le b)$.

INTERACTIVE · THE BELL CURVE

Change $\mu$ and $\sigma$ and watch position, height and width. The yellow area is the probability. Switch to “$\sigma$ rules” to see the three neighbourhoods.

EXAMPLE 1 · POINTS OF INFLECTION PROVED

Show that $\varphi(x) = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\,\mathrm{e}^{-x^2/2}$ has points of inflection at $x = \pm 1$.

Chain rule: $\varphi'(x) = -x\,\varphi(x)$. Product rule: $\varphi''(x) = -\varphi(x) - x\,\varphi'(x) = (x^2 - 1)\,\varphi(x)$.

Since $\varphi(x) > 0$, $\varphi''(x) = 0$ exactly for $x = \pm 1$, and $x^2 - 1$ changes sign there: points of inflection at $\pm 1 = \mu \pm \sigma$.

EXAMPLE 2 · PROBABILITY AS AREA

$X \sim N(0, 1)$. Calculate $P(-1 \le X \le 1)$ and $P(X > 2)$.

$P(-1 \le X \le 1) = \int_{-1}^{1} \varphi(x)\,\mathrm{d}x \approx 0.6827$ (CAS). There is no antiderivative in closed form, so you calculate with $\Phi$ or the CAS.

$P(X > 2) = 1 - \Phi(2) \approx 1 - 0.9772 = $ $0.0228$, so a good $2\%$.

EXERCISES

For $X \sim N(170, 8^2)$ (height in cm), state the position of the maximum and of the points of inflection of the density. How high is the maximum?

Maximum at $x = 170$, points of inflection at $162$ and $178$. Height $\varphi_{170;8}(170) = \tfrac{1}{8\sqrt{2\pi}} \approx 0.0499$.

Two bell curves have the same expected value. One is twice as wide. What holds for their maxima? Explain with the area.

Doubling $\sigma$ halves the factor $\tfrac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}$: the maximum is half as high. Both areas are $1$.

Check whether $f(x) = \tfrac{3}{4}(1 - x^2)$ for $-1 \le x \le 1$ (otherwise $0$) is a density, and calculate $P(X \ge 0.5)$.

$f \ge 0$ and $\int_{-1}^{1} \tfrac34(1 - x^2)\,\mathrm{d}x = \tfrac34 \cdot \tfrac43 = 1$: yes. $P(X \ge 0.5) = \tfrac34\left[x - \tfrac13 x^3\right]_{0.5}^{1} = \tfrac34\left(\tfrac23 - \tfrac{11}{24}\right) = \tfrac{5}{32} \approx 0.156$.

Show in general: the points of inflection of $\varphi_{\mu;\sigma}$ lie at $\mu \pm \sigma$.

Write $\varphi_{\mu;\sigma}(x) = c \cdot \mathrm{e}^{-u^2/2}$ with $u = \tfrac{x - \mu}{\sigma}$.

$\varphi' = -\tfrac{x - \mu}{\sigma^2}\varphi$, $\varphi'' = \left(\tfrac{(x - \mu)^2}{\sigma^4} - \tfrac{1}{\sigma^2}\right)\varphi = 0 \iff (x - \mu)^2 = \sigma^2 \iff x = \mu \pm \sigma$, with a change of sign.

The waiting time $T$ (in min) at a traffic light has the density $f(t) = \tfrac12$ for $0 \le t \le 2$. Calculate $E(T) = \int t\,f(t)\,\mathrm{d}t$ and $V(T) = \int (t - \mu)^2 f(t)\,\mathrm{d}t$.

$E(T) = \int_0^2 \tfrac t2\,\mathrm{d}t = 1$. $V(T) = \int_0^2 \tfrac12 (t - 1)^2\,\mathrm{d}t = \tfrac12 \cdot \tfrac23 = \tfrac13$, so $\sigma \approx 0.58$ min. This is how $E$ and $V$ carry over from sums to integrals.

TEST YOURSELF!

$P(-1 \le Z \le 1)$ for $Z \sim N(0, 1)$? Four decimal places.

$\Phi(1) - \Phi(-1)$

$X \sim N(170, 8^2)$: right point of inflection of the density?

$\mu + \sigma$

A point has no area.

UNIT 23 LESSONS

2Distribution function, standardising and $\sigma$ rules

The filling machine: $X \sim N(500, 4^2)$. How many bottles contain less than $492$ ml? $492$ lies exactly two standard deviations below $\mu$. For the standard normal distribution we know $P(Z \le -2) \approx 0.0228$. So it is a good $2\%$, without any new calculation, just by converting into standard deviations.

That is the idea of standardising: every normal distribution is a shifted and stretched standard normal distribution. With $z = \tfrac{x - \mu}{\sigma}$ you count how many standard deviations $x$ is away from the expected value. Then one single function, $\Phi$, is enough for all normal distributions. Conversely, limits, means and spreads can be found when a probability is given.

KEY POINT · DISTRIBUTION FUNCTION AND STANDARDISING

$F(x) = P(X \le x) = \displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{x} \varphi_{\mu;\sigma}(t)\,\mathrm{d}t = \Phi\!\left(\dfrac{x - \mu}{\sigma}\right)$

$P(a \le X \le b) = \Phi\!\left(\tfrac{b - \mu}{\sigma}\right) - \Phi\!\left(\tfrac{a - \mu}{\sigma}\right)$ · $P(X \ge a) = 1 - \Phi\!\left(\tfrac{a - \mu}{\sigma}\right)$ · $\Phi(-z) = 1 - \Phi(z)$

$\sigma$ rules: $68.3\%$ lie in $[\mu - \sigma, \mu + \sigma]$, $95.4\%$ in $\mu \pm 2\sigma$, $99.7\%$ in $\mu \pm 3\sigma$. Conversely: $90\%$ in $\mu \pm 1.64\sigma$, $95\%$ in $\mu \pm 1.96\sigma$, $99\%$ in $\mu \pm 2.58\sigma$.

Working backwards: if a probability is given, you look for the matching $z$ with invNorm on the CAS: $\Phi(z) = 0.95$ gives $z \approx 1.645$.

Sketch: draw the bell, mark $\mu$, shade the area you want. Then you see at once whether $\Phi$, $1 - \Phi$ or a difference is meant.

INTERACTIVE · THE FILLING MACHINE

Calculate with $\Phi$ instead of the area: switch to “Distribution function”. The probability you want is the difference in height of the graph there.

EXAMPLE 3 · BETWEEN TWO LIMITS

$X \sim N(500, 4^2)$. How many bottles contain between $495$ and $505$ ml?

$z_1 = \tfrac{495 - 500}{4} = -1.25$, $z_2 = 1.25$. $P = \Phi(1.25) - \Phi(-1.25) = 2\,\Phi(1.25) - 1 \approx 2 \cdot 0.8944 - 1$: $\approx 0.789$.

EXAMPLE 4 · LIMITING THE SPREAD

At most $1\%$ of the bottles may be below $490$ ml ($\mu = 500$). How large may $\sigma$ be at most?

$\Phi\!\left(\tfrac{490 - 500}{\sigma}\right) \le 0.01$. $\Phi(z) = 0.01$ for $z \approx -2.326$. So $-\tfrac{10}{\sigma} \le -2.326$: $\sigma \le \tfrac{10}{2.326} \approx 4.30$ ml.

EXERCISES

The height of young men is $N(180, 7^2)$-distributed (in cm). Calculate the proportion over $190$ cm and the proportion between $170$ and $185$ cm.

$1 - \Phi\!\left(\tfrac{10}{7}\right) \approx 1 - 0.9234 = 0.077$. $\Phi\!\left(\tfrac57\right) - \Phi\!\left(-\tfrac{10}{7}\right) \approx 0.7625 - 0.0766 = 0.686$.

Use the $\sigma$ rules to state without calculating: in which interval around $500$ ml do about $95\%$ of the fill quantities lie ($\sigma = 4$)?

$500 \pm 1.96 \cdot 4$, so about $[492.2, 507.8]$ ml.

Which fill quantity is exceeded by $95\%$ of the bottles ($\mu = 500$, $\sigma = 4$)?

We want $x$ with $P(X \le x) = 0.05$: $z \approx -1.645$, $x = 500 - 1.645 \cdot 4 \approx 493.4$ ml.

To which mean must the machine ($\sigma = 4$) be set so that only $1\%$ of the bottles are below $495$ ml?

$\tfrac{495 - \mu}{4} = -2.326$, so $\mu = 495 + 9.31 \approx 504.3$ ml.

In an exam the scores are roughly normally distributed. $15\%$ of the candidates have more than $80$ points, $10\%$ fewer than $40$. Find $\mu$ and $\sigma$.

Two conditions give two equations: $\tfrac{80 - \mu}{\sigma} = z_1$ and $\tfrac{40 - \mu}{\sigma} = z_2$.

$\Phi(z_1) = 0.85$: $z_1 \approx 1.036$. $\Phi(z_2) = 0.10$: $z_2 \approx -1.282$. $80 - \mu = 1.036\sigma$, $40 - \mu = -1.282\sigma$. Subtract: $40 = 2.318\sigma$, so $\sigma \approx 17.3$, $\mu \approx 62.1$.

TEST YOURSELF!

$X \sim N(500, 4^2)$: $P(X < 492)$? Four decimal places.

$\Phi(-2)$

$X \sim N(500, 4^2)$: $P(495 \le X \le 505)$? Three decimal places.

$2\,\Phi(1.25) - 1$

How large may $\sigma$ be at most if at most $1\%$ are to be below $490$ ml ($\mu = 500$)? One decimal place.

$10 / 2.326$

UNIT 33 LESSONS

3From the binomial to the normal distribution

$1000$ coin tosses: how likely are between $480$ and $520$ heads? Exactly, that is $41$ terms with huge binomial coefficients. But the histogram of $B(1000, 0.5)$ looks like a bell with $\mu = 500$ and $\sigma = \sqrt{250} \approx 15.8$. If you calculate the area under this bell from $479.5$ to $520.5$, you get $0.8052$. The exact value is $0.8052$.

Why $479.5$ and not $480$? Every bar of the histogram stands on an interval of width $1$ around its value $k$. So the bars from $480$ to $520$ reach from $479.5$ to $520.5$. This continuity correction makes the approximation considerably better. How good it is depends on $\sigma$: if $\sigma$ is small or $p$ is close to $0$ or $1$, the histogram is skewed, and the symmetric bell fits badly.

KEY POINT · THEOREM OF DE MOIVRE-LAPLACE

If $X \sim B(n, p)$ with $\mu = np$ and $\sigma = \sqrt{np(1 - p)}$, then for large $n$ approximately

$P(X \le k) \approx \Phi\!\left(\dfrac{k + 0.5 - \mu}{\sigma}\right)$ and $P(X = k) \approx \dfrac{1}{\sigma}\,\varphi\!\left(\dfrac{k - \mu}{\sigma}\right)$.

Rule of thumb (Laplace condition): the approximation is usable if $\sigma > 3$.

Today: the CAS also calculates $B(1000, 0.5)$ exactly. The approximation remains important because it shows why so many quantities are normally distributed: they are sums of many small, random influences.

Galton board: every ball goes through a Bernoulli chain. With many rows, the distribution over the bins becomes a bell.

INTERACTIVE · THE BELL OVER THE HISTOGRAM

Increase $n$ and watch the bars move up to the curve. Set $p = 0.05$: for small $n$ the histogram is skewed. In the standardised view all histograms lie over the same curve.

EXAMPLE 5 · A SINGLE PROBABILITY

$X \sim B(100, 0.5)$. Approximate $P(X = 50)$ and compare with the exact value.

$\mu = 50$, $\sigma = 5$: $P(X = 50) \approx \tfrac15\,\varphi(0) = \tfrac{1}{5\sqrt{2\pi}} \approx 0.0798$. Exactly: $\binom{100}{50} \cdot 0.5^{100} \approx 0.0796$. Deviation below $0.3\%$ of the value.

EXAMPLE 6 · WHERE THE APPROXIMATION WEAKENS

An airline sells $300$ tickets for $285$ seats. Each passenger turns up with $p = 0.92$. How likely is it that there are enough seats?

$\mu = 276$, $\sigma \approx 4.70 > 3$. Approximation: $\Phi\!\left(\tfrac{285.5 - 276}{4.70}\right) = \Phi(2.02) \approx 0.978$. Exactly with the CAS: $0.984$.

Usable, but less accurate: $p$ is close to $1$, the histogram is skewed.

EXERCISES

Check the Laplace condition for $B(50, 0.1)$, $B(200, 0.1)$ and $B(100, 0.5)$.

$\sigma = \sqrt{4.5} \approx 2.12$ (no), $\sqrt{18} \approx 4.24$ (yes), $5$ (yes).

$X \sim B(200, 0.3)$. Approximate $P(X \le 50)$ with and without the continuity correction. Exactly, $P(X \le 50) \approx 0.0695$.

$\mu = 60$, $\sigma = \sqrt{42} \approx 6.48$. With correction: $\Phi\!\left(\tfrac{50.5 - 60}{6.48}\right) = \Phi(-1.47) \approx 0.071$. Without: $\Phi(-1.54) \approx 0.062$. The correction is closer.

A dice is rolled $600$ times. In which interval, symmetric about the expected value, does the number of sixes lie with a probability of about $95\%$?

$\mu = 100$, $\sigma = \sqrt{600 \cdot \tfrac16 \cdot \tfrac56} \approx 9.13$. $100 \pm 1.96 \cdot 9.13$: about $[82, 118]$.

At least how often must you toss a coin so that the relative frequency of heads deviates from $0.5$ by at most $0.01$ with a probability of $95\%$?

For the relative frequency $H = \tfrac Xn$, $\sigma_H = \sqrt{\tfrac{p(1 - p)}{n}}$.

$1.96 \cdot \sqrt{\tfrac{0.25}{n}} \le 0.01 \iff \sqrt n \ge 98 \iff n \ge 9604$. For one percentage point of accuracy you need almost ten thousand tosses; the law of large numbers is slow.

TEST YOURSELF!

Approximation for $P(X = 50)$ with $X \sim B(100, 0.5)$? Four decimal places.

$\tfrac{1}{5\sqrt{2\pi}}$

Smallest number of tosses for $|H - 0.5| \le 0.01$ with $95\%$?

$(1.96 \cdot 0.5 / 0.01)^2$

For which distribution is the Laplace condition met?

$\sigma = \sqrt{18} > 3$

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

Apples of one variety weigh $180$ g on average with $\sigma = 15$ g (normally distributed). Apples under $160$ g go into juice. What proportion is that?

$\Phi\!\left(\tfrac{160 - 180}{15}\right) = \Phi(-1.33) \approx 0.091$, a good $9\%$.

Connecting with chapter E: calculate $\int_{-3}^{3} \varphi(x)\,\mathrm{d}x$ with the trapezium rule and $n = 6$ strips and compare with $0.9973$.

Values at $-3, \ldots, 3$: $0.0044$, $0.0540$, $0.2420$, $0.3989$, $0.2420$, $0.0540$, $0.0044$. Trapezium: $1 \cdot \left(\tfrac{0.0044 + 0.0044}{2} + 0.0540 + 0.2420 + 0.3989 + 0.2420 + 0.0540\right) \approx 0.995$. Very close already with six strips.

A machine cuts rods with $\sigma = 0.8$ mm. Tolerance: $200 \pm 1.5$ mm. How much scrap is there with $\mu = 200$ mm, and how much if the machine is set to $200.5$ mm by mistake?

$\mu = 200$: $1 - (\Phi(1.875) - \Phi(-1.875)) \approx 1 - 0.939 = 0.061$. $\mu = 200.5$: $1 - (\Phi(1.25) - \Phi(-2.5)) \approx 1 - (0.894 - 0.006) = 0.112$. The shift almost doubles the scrap.

A multiple-choice test has $100$ questions with $4$ answers each. If you only guess: how likely are at least $35$ correct answers? Approximate with de Moivre-Laplace and explain whether the approximation is allowed.

$\mu = 25$, $\sigma = \sqrt{18.75} \approx 4.33 > 3$: allowed. $P(X \ge 35) = 1 - P(X \le 34) \approx 1 - \Phi\!\left(\tfrac{34.5 - 25}{4.33}\right) = 1 - \Phi(2.19) \approx 0.014$.

EXCURSIONHISTORY

The bell in your wallet

On 12 November 1733 the mathematician Abraham de Moivre (1667–1754), a Huguenot who had fled to London, handed friends a seven-page Latin booklet: Approximatio ad Summam Terminorum Binomii (a + b)n in Seriem expansi. In it he approximates the terms of the binomial for large $n$ by a curve that we now call the bell curve, and recognises the standard deviation as the natural unit of spread. Only two copies of the booklet survive. He included an English version of his own in 1738 in the second edition of his book The Doctrine of Chances.

Even so, the curve got its name from someone else: Carl Friedrich Gauss used it in 1809 in his Theoria motus corporum coelestium as the law of observational errors, when he calculated planetary orbits from inaccurate measurements. In 1812 Pierre-Simon Laplace proved a general form of the limit theorem in his Théorie analytique des probabilités: sums of many small random influences are approximately normally distributed.

From 1991 to the end of 2001 every ten-mark note in Germany showed Gauss, with houses of Göttingen behind him and next to him the bell curve with its formula. The Bundesbank first issued it on 16 April 1991. Probably never before was a formula from probability theory in so many pockets so often.

Sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics (St Andrews), “Abraham de Moivre”; W. E. Deming, Nature 132 (1933), p. 713; Deutsche Bundesbank, DM banknotes series BBK III.
